One of the most difficult jobs that a community manager has to do is to enforce a Code of Conduct (CoC).

A Code of Conduct (CoC) is a set of guidelines provided for individuals or participants in the same environment to interact and communicate with each other in a way that protects and respects their values while engaging with each other or building a network.

It is one of the most important documents for an open-source project. CoCs ensure individuals in communities feel safe and respected, but also they can form an important document when limiting the liability of developers of open-source software.
In this blog, we’re going to talk about some simple rules to help community managers enforce their Code of Conduct.
1. Make the document public and findable

Your CoC should be easily visible in your community. When someone joins a community for the first time, it should be one of the first things they see. This is important to ensure your community members know what is and is not allowed in your community. We recommend having a copy of your community’s CoC on every GitHub repository, on any platforms you use for asynchronous communication (e.g., Slack or Zoom), and linked in any documents for (online or offline) events you may run.

Having a public CoC is vital for transparent enforcement. Someone cannot be accused of breaking a rule they didn’t know existed. Ensuring the CoC is visible protects you from any disagreements that may arise if a community member claims they didn’t see it.

It is very difficult to enforce rules that are vague, so ensure your rules are clear and direct. For example, compare “Do not harass other community members in private or public” and “Do not bother other members”. The first is a clear, unambiguous rule. If one member is harassing another, the degree of harassment does not matter, and harassment, by definition, means “unwanted behavior”, there is a clear line between wanted and unwanted attention. In contrast, it is very easy to accidentally annoy someone else without realising.

A privilege but a challenge of being a community manager is working with people from all over the world. We all have different cultures and upbringings that affect how we interact with each other. For example, in the Netherlands, negative feedback is given in a very direct manner, but for a Korean visitor, this sort of communication would be perceived as rude and potentially arrogant (see Erin Meyer’s blog post for more examples). Community managers should take this into account when judging if something is a breach of the CoC.

This might seem obvious, but it’s worth stating, to enforce your CoC you have to enforce the CoC. Do not deviate from the CoC that is shared with your community. The worst thing you can do is make exceptions to the rule, this creates confusion and risks “playing favourites”. If someone breaks a rule, go through whatever process you created. This may be as simple as sending a private message telling the person they broke a rule. Just ensure that the consequences are very clearly stated and enforced. Enforcing rules is genuinely difficult, but always remember that not enforcing rules can lead other community members to feel excluded or unsafe, which can inadvertently set the tone for how your community is perceived.

Whilst community managers often appear to be omnipresent and omniscient within their community, unfortunately, this is not actually the case. Rules could be broken in a channel you haven’t checked in a while, in a direct message between two members, in a breakout room on Zoom, or at an in-person event. To ensure these are not missed you should encourage community members to report all breaches of your Code of Conduct. Ideally you should allow anonymity, for example, you could create a form that allows people to share breaches of the CoC whilst remaining anonymous. However, if this is not possible, then simply provide an email address where any breaches should be reported to.

Humans thrive on predictability. When people know what to generally expect, they are able to tailor their actions accordingly and adapt better. Making use of an existing CoC creates familiarity for community members who may be part of many other communities. There are several existing templates that can be used for a CoC, the most commonly used at the moment is the Contributor Covenant v2. The Organization for Ethical Source has also just released version 3 of the Contributor Covenant.
7. Have a code of conduct committee

To minimise the risk of bias and favoritism, or accusations of these, you might consider having a Code of Conduct committee who make all enforcement decisions together. Members of your committee should be clearly stated in a CoC and each member of the committee should have equal opportunity to discuss a case and equal voting rights when it comes to making decisions. Committees should have at least three members, this is important in case the offender is a member of the committee. Structures should also be put in place to allow community members to appeal decisions and to report the committee should a decision be frowned upon.
A Code of Conduct(CoC) is an essential document in a community. Creating it is one thing, and enforcing it is another. Enforcing your Code of Conduct is vital to creating a safe and happy community.
